extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and competition mathematics students (readers solving polynomial and functional-equation problems)
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and analyze contest-style problems about polynomials and functional equations, using algebraic, number-theoretic, complex-analytic and functional-equation techniques. The text gives worked solutions and heuristics for deducing structure, contradictions, and classifications of possible solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of roots of unity / cyclotomic evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate polynomials at roots of unity (e.g., primitive 5th roots) to obtain values at several distinct points; use that a low-degree polynomial taking the same value at many roots of unity must be constant, or that divisibility by cyclotomic factors follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In problem 35 set ω a 5th root of unity; if a degree ≤3 polynomial r(x) takes the value 5 at ω, ω^2, ω^3, ω^4 then r≡5. Another approach uses x^5−1 factorization: (x−1)f(x)=x^5−1 to deduce remainder. Use these to determine remainders or divisibility by x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal principle on zeros
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a zero of maximal modulus (distance from origin) and apply the functional/polynomial relations to its images to derive contradictions or force particular zeros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (problem 37): let z be a zero of maximal distance; applying f-relations to z, z^2+z+1, z^2−z+1 shows z must be 0 or on unit circle and led to z=±i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vieta relations to connect coefficients and roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare coefficients with expanded factorization to equate symmetric sums and products of roots with polynomial coefficients, then use these identities to deduce constraints (parity, divisibility, possible root products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout (e.g., problems 31, 39, 56): equate sums x1+x2+... = −a, pairwise sums = b, product = ±c and deduce odd/even or obtain polynomial equations for combinations like ab, u=ab leading to further elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity and modular divisibility arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parity (odd/even) or modular arithmetic constraints on coefficients and values at integers to derive contradictions or force divisibility properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem 31 deduces b and c must be odd from divisibility of integer zeros; problem 47 uses values modulo 7 at several integer inputs to conclude 7 divides all coefficients; problem 74 uses Fermat's little theorem mod 5 to rule out factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume factorization and evaluate at special points to force contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a polynomial factors nontrivially, evaluate the factors at specially chosen points (e.g., at root locations, integers) to obtain impossible multiplicative identities (e.g., expressing 1 as product of distinct integers) or coefficient contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem 32 (evaluate at x=a,b to deduce p(a)q(a)=1 leading to divisibility contradictions), problem 58 (f(ai)=±1 and degree considerations give contradiction), problem 45 (if integer root z then product of distinct factors equals 1 impossible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution and reciprocal / variable-change transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply algebraic substitutions (reciprocal, scale, x→ax, x→x+1/x, x→2 cos t, etc.) to convert problems into more tractable forms or reduce degree / symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem 29 divides by a^2 x^2 and sets x/a − a/x; problem 56 uses substitution y=ax to make zeros integers; problem 68 sets x=2 cos t to exploit doubling formulas; reciprocal substitutions reduce reciprocal equations to quadratics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding, maxima/minima and inequality techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use derivative tests or elementary inequalities (AM-GM, triangle inequality, Cauchy–Schwarz) and evaluate on intervals (e.g., |x|≤1) to bound polynomial coefficients or values and thereby classify extremal polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem 48 bounds |f(x)|≤1 on |x|≤1 and uses maxima of derivative at endpoints; problem 66 uses |u|,|v|≤1 ⇒ |u−v|≤2 and combines inequalities to bound quadratic coefficients and show extremal cases; problem 49 uses positivity of even-degree polynomial to show no real roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional-equation solution strategies (Cauchy/Jensen/log/exp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard methods: reduce multiplicative to additive forms via logs, use substitution x=e^u to convert f(xy)=f(x)+f(y) to Cauchy, determine values on rationals then extend to reals by continuity/monotonicity/boundedness; take logarithms for f(x+y)=f(x)f(y) analogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples E1–E5: differentiability on x>0 gives f(x)=c ln x for f(xy)=f(x)+f(y); positivity and log transform give f(x)=e^{cx} for f(x+y)=f(x)f(y); Jensen's equation handled by reducing to additive Cauchy plus constant shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iteration to generate infinite sequences and derive contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the functional relation to iterate from a root/value and produce infinitely many distinct zeros or values unless constrained; deduce impossible infinite zero sets for polynomials or force modulus restrictions on roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (problem 57): if α is a zero then define α_{n+1}=2α_n^3+α_n; triangle inequality shows |α|>1 would yield infinitely many zeros contradiction, so |α|=1 and further constraints force α^2=−1; similar iterative arguments appear for other functional forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry reduction via elementary symmetric functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For symmetric polynomial equations in several variables, switch to elementary symmetric variables (sums and products) to reduce degree and solve Diophantine possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (problem 62): replace x+y=u and xy=v to transform symmetric cubic relation into an equation in u and v, then analyze integer solutions for parameter t with u=2t and solve for v producing finite possible integer pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial-division and remainder-degree arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a polynomial as quotient·divisor + remainder and use degree constraints plus evaluations at special points to determine the remainder explicitly (often constant) or force divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem 35 writes x^20+...+1=(x^4+...+1)q(x)+r(x) and evaluates at 4th-degree roots to show remainder r≡5; problem 42 computes remainder of x^1959−1 upon division by specific quadratics by evaluating at i, −i, ω, ω^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discriminant / critical-point analysis to bound number of real roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute derivative/critical points and discriminant conditions to decide monotonicity or necessary/sufficient conditions for multiple real zeros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem 50 computes critical points of cubic using derivative 3x^2+2px+q and shows p^2<3q ⇒ no three real zeros; problem 79 computes discriminant of quadratic in x to find allowable y values giving real solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducibility and degree-modulus arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine modulus (prime) arguments and degree/product bounds to show a polynomial cannot factor over Z or cannot have low-degree integer-factorization, often using bounds on product of roots or Fermat-type congruences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: problem 73 uses product of roots and size bounds to show impossibility of factoring into degrees <105; problem 74 uses Fermat's little theorem to force divisibility by 5, contradicting assumptions and excluding certain factor forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric / Chebyshev substitution for iterative polynomial equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use x=2 cos t and the cosine duplication identities to transform polynomial iteration P_n(x)=x into trigonometric equations 2 cos(2^n t)=2 cos t; deduce number and explicit values of real solutions via angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (problem 68): setting x=2 cos t converts P_k(x) into 2 cos(2^k t) and P_n(x)=x turns into 2^n t ≡ ±t (mod 2π), giving explicit 2n distinct x-values 2 cos(t) that satisfy the iteration.
